by: Eric S. Téllez

This tutorial walks through the embedded API end to end, using paragraphs from *Frankenstein*
(bundled in this package's own test data) as a single running example: dense vector search
with LSI-derived embeddings, full-text search with BM25 and TF-IDF, soft deletes, filtering,
calibrating for a target recall, closing/reopening a project, and the "expensive", whole-dataset
operations (`allknn`, `fft`, `closestpairs`, `bichromatic_kclosestpairs`) that only make sense
once you actually have a project's worth of data to run them against. For a shorter,
bare-minimum first look, see the repository's [README](../../README.md).

## Installation

`SimilaritySearchEngine.jl` isn't registered yet — develop it from a local checkout (or a
git URL) alongside its own dependencies:

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.develop(path="path/to/SimilaritySearchEngine.jl")
```

## The Frankenstein dataset

This package's own test suite ships `test/data/frankenstein.jsonl` — one JSON object per
paragraph of the novel, already split, cleaned, and annotated by
`test/generate_datasets.jl`. Loading it gives you a `Vector` of plain `Dict`s, each already
shaped to match [`Schema.MetadataRecord`](../architecture.qmd)'s record/data/metadata
contract:

```julia
using JSON

items = [JSON.parse(l) for l in readlines("test/data/frankenstein.jsonl")]
length(items)  # 724 paragraphs
first(keys(items[1]))
```

Each item has:

- `"text"`: the paragraph itself (raw data — never duplicated into metadata).
- `"doc_id"`: an external id like `"frankenstein_1"` (the record's fixed external-id field).
- `"keywords"`: character names detected in that paragraph, e.g. `["Elizabeth", "Victor"]`
  (the record's fixed, indexed tag field).
- `"ref"`: the *previous* paragraph's `doc_id` (the record's fixed, unvalidated reference
  field — a forward/backward link, here used to keep narrative order available even
  though nothing enforces `ref`s point at something that exists).
- `"word_count"`/`"verb_count"`: free-form metadata (`meta`) — anything not a reserved key
  (`vector`/`text`/`doc_id`/`keywords`/`ref`) falls through here as-is, flat, with no
  wrapper key of its own.

There's no `"vector"` key yet — that's the dense section's job, below.

## Dense vectors with LSI (SearchGraph)

`create_project` makes a brand-new project directly on disk, at `<workdir>/<dataset>`. By
default it builds a `SearchGraph` (an approximate, self-tuning index) autotuning toward
`minrecall=0.9`:

```julia
using SimilaritySearchEngine
using SimilaritySearch: SearchGraph

workdir = mktempdir()
h = create_project(workdir, "frankenstein_dense"; engine=DenseEngine, backend=SearchGraph, minrecall=0.9)
```

### Getting real dense vectors quickly, with LSI

A `SearchGraph` project needs `Vector{Float32}`s to index — if you don't already have an
embedding model at hand, `TextSearch.jl`'s Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI) gives you real,
meaningful dense vectors straight from a text corpus, in-process, with no external model
or API call: fit once on your corpus, then project any text (an indexed paragraph, or a
brand-new query) into that same dense space.

```julia
using TextSearch: LatentSemanticIndexing, outdim
using TextSearch.LSI: vectorize

corpus = [it["text"] for it in items]
lsi = LatentSemanticIndexing(corpus; maxoutdim=128, verbose=false)
outdim(lsi)  # 128 -- the full corpus easily supports it
```

(`maxoutdim` is a cap, not a guarantee: `outdim(lsi)` is `min(maxoutdim, vocabulary size,
corpus size)` — a tiny placeholder corpus of just a handful of documents would yield far
fewer dimensions than requested; 724 real paragraphs comfortably reach 128.)

Items are appended as a `Vector` of dicts, each carrying a `"vector"` key plus the record
fields loaded above. We'll only insert the *first half* of the book here, and hold the
second half back in reserve, unindexed, for the bichromatic example further down:

```julia
half = length(items) ÷ 2

batch = [
    DenseItem(vectorize(lsi, it["text"]);
              doc_id = it["doc_id"], keywords = it["keywords"], refs = it["ref"],
              meta = Dict{String,Any}("word_count" => it["word_count"],
                                      "verb_count" => it["verb_count"]))
    for it in items[1:half]
]
append_items!(h, batch)  # inserted == 362
```

(`append_items!` accepts a batch — passing many items in one call amortizes better than
one `append_items!` call per item, though both work; see
[Architecture](../architecture.qmd) for why batch size matters even more for a dense
project specifically.)

### Indexing the staged vectors

For a `SearchGraph` project, `append_items!` only *stages* raw vectors — cheaply, and
durably, but without doing any of the (expensive) graph-connection work. Nothing is
searchable yet:

```julia
search(h, vectorize(lsi, "the monster and its creator"), 5)  # Vector{...}[] -- empty, nothing indexed yet
```

`index!` explicitly builds the graph over whatever's been staged since the last call (or
since creation) — call it once you're ready for staged items to become searchable,
whether that's right after every `append_items!` call, on your own periodic schedule, or
just once before a batch of queries:

```julia
index!(h)
```

It's cheap to call again later with nothing new staged (a no-op), and only ever processes
the backlog — call it as often as fits your workflow. Searching now finds the 362 staged
paragraphs:

```julia
query = vectorize(lsi, "the monster and its creator")
results = search(h, query, 5)
for r in results
    println(r.doc_id, " => distance ", r.distance)
end
```

Pass a `filter` predicate — a plain `(record, meta) -> Bool` function over each
candidate's fixed `Schema.MetadataRecord` (`doc_id`, `keywords`, `refs`, ...) and its
free-form `meta` (whatever else you appended it with) — to restrict results without
building a separate query language:

```julia
mentions_someone = search(h, query, 5; filter = (record, meta) -> !isempty(record.keywords))
```

### Soft deletes

`delete_item!` marks a document as logically deleted; the index itself is untouched. It
takes the internal `_id` (the position `add_item!` assigned it, e.g. as returned in a
search result's `doc_id` field), not the `"doc_id"` you supplied when appending:

```julia
delete_item!(h, 1)  # internal _id 1, not any "doc_id"/metadata value

results = search(h, query, 5)
first(results).deleted  # true if internal _id 1 made the top-5 candidates
```

A soft-deleted candidate is *reported*, not hidden and backfilled — if you need `k` live
results after filtering out deletions, overfetch and page yourself, or let
`SimilaritySearchServer`'s cursor layer do it for you.

### Calibrating for a target recall

`calibrate!` runs a real hyperparameter search and persists the result, so a later
`search(...; minrecall=0.95)` call can serve that target recall from a tuned `BeamSearch`
instead of the constructor's default:

```julia
calibrate!(h; levels=[0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.97])
precise = search(h, query, 5; minrecall=0.95)
```

It needs a reasonably sized project to have anything meaningful to search against and
tune over — this 724-paragraph corpus is plenty; a toy corpus of just a handful of items
would print a wall of "ignoring configuration"/"too few queries" warnings instead (harmless,
just noisy), since there wouldn't be enough distinct items for its own internal sample
queries.

### Closing and reopening

```julia
close_project!(h)

h2 = open_project(workdir, "frankenstein_dense")
same_query_results = search(h2, query, 5)
close_project!(h2)
```

Every insertion was already persisted incrementally as it happened (see
[Architecture](../architecture.qmd)), so `close_project!` only needs to flush anything
still pending for index kinds that don't persist incrementally on their own. Staging and
indexing are tracked separately, too: reopening restores exactly how far `index!` actually
got, not just how much was staged -- had we appended more items after the last `index!`
call above and closed without indexing them, they'd still be there (staged, with their
metadata already fetchable) after reopening, just not yet searchable, waiting on a future
`index!` call to catch them up.

`same_query_results` will be *close to*, but isn't guaranteed to be byte-identical to, the
`results` from before closing: `SearchGraph` is an approximate index, and rebuilding it
from persisted vectors (`open_project` replays every insertion in the same order) doesn't
guarantee an identical internal graph topology to the one built live, so its beam search
can explore a slightly different candidate set — expect the same ballpark of hits (often
exactly the same), not a bitwise-reproducible top-`k`, unless you calibrate and search
with an explicit `minrecall` on both sides.

## Full-text search with BM25

Text projects work the same way as dense ones, just with a `"text"` key instead of
`"vector"`, and `ftsearch` instead of `search` — and, since the redesign that decoupled
staging from indexing, the *exact same* `append_items!`(stage)/`index!`(build) shape as a
dense project, not a separate training step. `BM25InvertedFile` scores via BM25 over raw
bags-of-words:

```julia
using TextSearch: BM25InvertedFile

# `textmodel` is required for a text project -- see the next section for what the
# alternative is and why neither is a default
hb = create_project(workdir, "frankenstein_bm25"; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=BM25InvertedFile,
                    textmodel=FitFromCorpus())

append_items!(hb, [
    TextItem(it["text"]; doc_id = it["doc_id"], keywords = it["keywords"])
    for it in items[1:200]
])  # only stages raw text -- nothing searchable yet

index!(hb)  # first call: fits the TextProfile from everything staged so far, then indexes it

hits = ftsearch(hb, "monster creature fear", 5)
for r in hits
    println(r.doc_id, " => distance ", r.distance)
end

close_project!(hb)
```

`index!`'s *first* call on a text project doubles as training: it fits a `TextProfile`
(vocabulary, tf-idf weights, lineage) and builds the real `BM25InvertedFile` from every item
staged so far, then encodes/indexes that same backlog — there's no separate training entry
point or "must be trained first" error. Every later `index!` call just catches up whatever's
been staged since, exactly like the dense case: idempotent, safe to call repeatedly, a cheap
no-op when nothing new is staged.

Tokens never seen at that first `index!` call are out-of-vocabulary on every later append
and silently dropped, so what you've staged before it has to be representative of the text
you'll keep appending. `text_profile(hb)` hands you the fitted model, and `save_profile` writes
it out for reuse — but the real fix for a project that keeps growing is the next section.

## Choosing the text model

`textmodel` above was not decoration. Creating a text project requires it, and there is no
default:

```julia
create_project(workdir, "oops"; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=BM25InvertedFile)
# ERROR: a text project (BM25InvertedFile) needs an explicit `textmodel`, because the ways to
#        get a vocabulary are not interchangeable and the cheap one cannot be undone later: ...
```

Three forms answer *where the vocabulary comes from*. They are not variations on one setting,
and the order below is the order worth preferring them in.

### `DefaultProfile` — start from a language, adapt to your corpus

```julia
hes = create_project(workdir, "noticias"; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=BM25InvertedFile,
                     textmodel=DefaultProfile(:es))
```

This is the one to reach for. At the first `index!` call it loads the published Spanish
paragraph profile and *refits* it against whatever you have staged: the base's token counts are
blended with your corpus's, the weights recomputed, and the stopword set, lemma map and
expansion network inherited. No embedding is fitted, which is what makes a refit cheap next to a
fit.

Be clear about what the refit does and does not give you, because the obvious guess is wrong.
Measured on the published English profile: 335,336 tokens in the base, 12,238 after refitting
against an 800-document sample, of which 2,649 are tokens the sample never held. Fitting on that
sample alone would have given 9,589. So the refit **narrows** to your corpus's vocabulary,
widened about a quarter by the base — it is not language-wide coverage. What you inherit is the
part your own corpus cannot produce: weights calibrated over millions of paragraphs, and (for
that base) 96 stopwords, 16,661 lemmas and 10,655 expansion entries.

If coverage is what you need — terms a later batch will introduce that today's corpus has never
seen — pass `refit=false` and index against the base untouched, all 335,336 tokens, with
Wikipedia's weights rather than yours. Calibration or coverage: the two forms answer different
questions.

The profile is resolved from the library `textsearch install` maintains, under
`~/.textsearch/profiles/`. Nothing is bundled or downloaded — the profiles are 70–160 MB — and
if the one you asked for is not installed the error says so and prints the command that
installs it. `refit=false` indexes against the base untouched, and `nickname=` points at any
installed profile instead of the per-language default.

### `FitFromCorpus` — deliberately no base profile

Fit the model from this project's own staged corpus, at the first `index!` call. This is the
explicit way to say "I have nothing pre-fitted", and it is the weakest of the three:

```julia
using TextSearch: NormalizationConfig

hf = create_project(workdir, "noticias_propias"; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=BM25InvertedFile,
    textmodel=FitFromCorpus(TextConfig(normalization=NormalizationConfig(lc=false, del_diac=false),
                                       language=:es);
                            min_ndocs=3, stopwords=0.9))
```

Its argument is the corpus-independent policy — normalization, tokenization, and the `language`
the corpus is in. The default `TextConfig()` lowercases and strips diacritics, which is usually
right for English and throws away a distinction that matters in Spanish.

The fit itself is handed whole to `TextSearch.fit_profile`; this package does not fit profiles.
That has a consequence worth stating plainly: there is no cheap variant of that pipeline. Every
fit runs an LSI over the sample, derives an expansion network from it and clusters a lemma map
from the same embeddings. Measured on 3,000 paragraphs it takes about 49 seconds, against 0.2
for a bare vocabulary-and-weights pass — which is why `max_documents` exists:

| option | what it does |
|---|---|
| `max_documents` | read at most this many documents (1,000 by default), sampled by an even stride across the corpus rather than taken from the front. `0` lifts the cap |
| `min_ndocs` | drop a token seen in fewer documents than this, before the encoder runs. Not cosmetic: the expansion network is an all-pairs kNN over the vocabulary |
| `stopwords` | a document-frequency threshold in `(0, 1]`; tokens above it are dropped and the vocabulary recounted without them. A second pass over the sample |
| `encoder`, `expansion`, `lemmas` | the library's own option groups, as `NamedTuple`s — `encoder=(; outdim=128)`, `lemmas=(; apply=true)` |

The cap bounds the cost and cuts against the one thing this path is already worst at: a
vocabulary from 1,000 sampled documents is thin, so *more* of what you append later is
out-of-vocabulary and silently dropped. That is the trade, and it is why the section above
exists.

### `BaseProfile` — a model fitted elsewhere

```julia
hp = create_project(workdir, "noticias_wiki"; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=BM25InvertedFile,
                    textmodel=BaseProfile(load_profile("wiki20231101-es.zip")))
```

This trains the project before its first item is ever staged, and is what `DefaultProfile`
does underneath once it has resolved and refitted — use this form when you already hold the
file, or when you want the base used exactly as it is. To load a profile but decline one of its
artifacts, change the profile rather than the project:
`BaseProfile(with_applied(p; lemmas=false))`.

Either way the spec is persisted with the project and restored verbatim by `open_project`. And
a project that fitted its own model can export it for the next one to index against:

```julia
save_profile("mi-perfil", text_profile(hes))
create_project(workdir, "hermano"; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=BM25InvertedFile,
               textmodel=BaseProfile(load_profile("mi-perfil")))
```

Passing a `textmodel` to a *dense* project is an error rather than an ignored keyword — there
is no reading under which it does anything.

## Correcting and widening a query

A query travels with a `QueryPolicy`, because whether to correct a misspelling or widen a
search is a guess about what the person meant — a property of the query, not of the index:

```julia
ftsearch(hes, "musica clasica", 5)                                   # :auto (the default)
ftsearch(hes, "musica clasica", 5; policy=QueryPolicy(correction=:off))   # exactly as typed
```

Under `:auto`, a typed token is bridged to another spelling of the same word only where the
evidence says the typed one is wrong — it is absent from the vocabulary, or far rarer than
another spelling of it. On a corpus indexed with `del_diac=false`, `musica` reaches `música`
and `clasica` reaches `clásica`; a correctly typed query is left alone. Under the default
`TextConfig()` this is inert, since folding case and diacritics already collapsed those
spellings into one.

A search that silently substitutes what was asked for owes the caller a way to see it, which
is `ftexplain`:

```julia
julia> ftexplain(hes, "musica clasica")
2-element Vector{String}:
 "musica is in 1 document against música's 60, so it reads as a misspelling; searched as música (variant) instead"
 "clasica is in 1 document against clásica's 60, so it reads as a misspelling; searched as clásica (variant) instead"
```

`QueryPolicy` also carries `expansion`/`expansion_k`, which widen the query with the
profile's query-expansion network — inert unless the project was created from a profile that
carries one.

## Full-text search with TF-IDF

`TextInvertedFile` is the other text index kind: a classic TF-IDF-weighted (`IdfWeighting` +
`TfWeighting`) inverted index, cosine distance by default — a good baseline to compare
against BM25's ranking on the same corpus. (`InvertedFile` selects the same engine and is
accepted interchangeably; `TextInvertedFile` is the name of what actually gets built.)

```julia
using TextSearch: TextInvertedFile

ht = create_project(workdir, "frankenstein_tfidf"; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=TextInvertedFile,
                    textmodel=FitFromCorpus())

append_items!(ht, [
    TextItem(it["text"]; doc_id = it["doc_id"], keywords = it["keywords"])
    for it in items[1:200]
])

index!(ht)  # same stage-then-index shape as BM25 above

hits = ftsearch(ht, "monster creature fear", 5)
for r in hits
    println(r.doc_id, " => distance ", r.distance)
end

close_project!(ht)
```

Same insertion/search shape as BM25 — only `backend` changes — so switching between the
two to compare rankings on your own corpus is a one-line change.

## Expensive, whole-dataset operations

`allknn`, `fft`, `closestpairs`, and `bichromatic_kclosestpairs` all run synchronously,
in-process — no job queue, unlike the HTTP API's `POST /api/v1/jobs/allknn` — which is
exactly why they're grouped here as their own section: each one does real work
proportional to the *whole* dataset (or two datasets, for the bichromatic case), so run
them against a project you actually want an answer for, not casually inside a hot loop.
All four need a dense (`SearchGraph`) project; reopen the one from the LSI section above
if you closed it:

```julia
h2 = open_project(workdir, "frankenstein_dense")
```

### All-pairs nearest neighbors

`allknn` runs `SimilaritySearch.jl`'s batch all-nearest-neighbors — every item's own
top-`k` neighbors, all at once:

```julia
neighbors = allknn(h2; k=5)
first(neighbors)  # (id=1, neighbors=[...], dists=[...])
```

`id`/`neighbors` are internal `_id`s (1-based insertion position), not `doc_id`s — see
[Metadata lookups](#metadata-lookups) to resolve them back to paragraph text.

### Farthest-first traversal (diverse sampling)

`fft` picks `k` items that are as far from each other as possible — useful for a diverse,
representative sample of the corpus (e.g. candidate cluster centers), rather than the
"closest to a query" shape every other search here has:

```julia
R = fft(h2, 8; verbose=false)
R.centers      # 8 well-separated internal _ids
R.separation   # the smallest distance between two of those 8
R.covering     # the largest distance from any item to its nearest one
```

`R.assign[i]` says which of the 8 item `i` belongs to — a **position** in `R.centers`, from
`1` to `8`, so `R.centers[R.assign[i]]` is that center's own `_id` and `R.assigndist[i]` is
how far item `i` sits from it. That makes `fft` double as a quick partition of the corpus
around `k` spread-out seeds.

### `k` closest pairs (near-duplicates and echoes within one corpus)

`closestpairs` finds the `k` globally closest pairs of items *within* a single project —
useful for spotting near-duplicate or strongly echoing passages:

```julia
pairs = closestpairs(h2; k=5)
for (i, j, d) in pairs
    ri = get_metadata(h2.project, i)
    rj = get_metadata(h2.project, j)
    println(ri.doc_id, " <-> ", rj.doc_id, "  dist=", d)
    println("  A: ", first(items[i]["text"], 90))
    println("  B: ", first(items[j]["text"], 90))
end
```

Running this against the first half of the novel (`h2` as built above) turns up passages
like Elizabeth's account of Justine's trial echoed a few paragraphs later almost verbatim,
at a distance well below typical unrelated pairs — exactly the kind of near-duplicate/
strong echo this function is for.

### Bichromatic `k` closest pairs (across two collections)

`bichromatic_kclosestpairs` finds the `k` closest pairs *between* a project's own index and
a second, separate collection of vectors that isn't indexed by anything — here, the first
half of the novel (already indexed as `h2`, see above) against the second half's vectors
(computed with the same LSI model, but never inserted anywhere):

```julia
using SimilaritySearch: MatrixDatabase

second_half_vectors = [vectorize(lsi, it["text"]) for it in items[(half + 1):end]]
B = MatrixDatabase(hcat(second_half_vectors...))

pairs = bichromatic_kclosestpairs(h2, B; k=5)
for (i, j, d) in pairs
    ri = get_metadata(h2.project, i)             # i is h2's own internal _id
    other = items[half + j]                       # j is B's own 1-based position
    println(ri.doc_id, " <-> ", other["doc_id"], "  dist=", d)
    println("  A: ", first(items[i]["text"], 100))
    println("  B: ", first(other["text"], 100))
end
```

On the real novel, this surfaces thematically matched passages across the two halves —
e.g. Walton's opening framing letters about a "strange accident" pairing with an equally
breathless first-person account much later in the book, well below the distance of an
unrelated cross-half pair.

## Metadata lookups

`fetch_items` and `exists` accept either the internal `_id` (an integer, or a string of
one, e.g. `"1"`) or the `doc_id` you supplied when appending. `fetch_items` returns a
`StoredItem` per resolved id — the record's fixed fields, its free-form `meta`, and the
`payload` that was actually indexed:

```julia
it = only(fetch_items(h2, ["frankenstein_2"]))
it._id            # 2
it.doc_id         # "frankenstein_2"
it.keywords       # ["Chapter", ...]
it.meta["word_count"]
it.payload        # the vector this project indexed (a paragraph, in a text project)

exists(h2, [1, "some-doc-id"])   # Vector{ExistsResult}: (id, exists, deleted)
```

An id that resolves to nothing is dropped by `fetch_items` (so the result can be shorter
than what you asked for) and reported by `exists` (so it is always the same length).

`get_metadata(h2.project, _id)` (used in the closest-pairs examples above) is the lower-level
single-record accessor `fetch_items` itself is built on — it returns just the
`Schema.MetadataRecord` (no `meta` merged in), which is all those examples needed.
